summary: This informational document defines a deterministic procedure for generating digital signatures. The signatures are compatible with standard DSA and ECDSA and verifiers need not know about the procedure. They retain the security properties of normal signatures but can be easier to implement in some environments.

plainLanguage.summary: Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) signatures normally depend on a new random value each time. This RFC derives that value from the private key and message, so signing needs no random source at that moment.

subtitle: A deterministic way to generate DSA and ECDSA signatures without signing-time randomness.

tldr.problem: DSA and ECDSA normally require a fresh, high-quality random value for each signature, which can be difficult to provide and test.
tldr.mechanism: The procedure derives the per-signature value from the private key and hashed message using HMAC, then performs standard DSA or ECDSA signing.
tldr.outcome: The signatures work with unmodified verifiers, but key-pair generation still requires strong randomness.

today: RFC 6979 is Informational, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC Editor's status text makes no claim about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Why Make Signature Generation Deterministic
sections.content:
DSA and ECDSA require a fresh value k for each signature. If the random source produces biased or repeated values, attackers may recover the signing key. Some devices have difficulty generating strong randomness during operation.

RFC 6979 defines a deterministic method for choosing k from the private key and message hash. The resulting signatures remain compatible with standard DSA and ECDSA verification.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak random value can expose a signing key. This procedure avoids needing a new random value while creating each signature.

sections.title: How DSA and ECDSA Signatures Use k
sections.content:
In DSA and ECDSA, the signer hashes the message and combines that hash with the private key and the per-signature value k. The algorithm produces two values, r and s, which form the signature.

The RFC defines conversions between bit strings, integers, and octet strings so that implementations handle the hash and key consistently. Deterministic DSA and ECDSA use the same signing steps; only the generation of k changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature still uses the standard DSA or ECDSA calculation. The RFC changes only how the signer obtains its one-time value.

sections.title: Generating k with HMAC
sections.content:
The signer hashes the message, initializes the HMAC state, and mixes in the private key and a converted form of the message hash. It then generates candidate values for k until it obtains one in the required range that produces a nonzero r.

The candidate is checked against the group order rather than reduced modulo it, because reduction would introduce bias. The RFC also gives an equivalent description using HMAC_DRBG.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer feeds the private key and message hash into HMAC to produce candidate values. It accepts a candidate only when it meets the signing algorithm's rules.

sections.title: Rationale and Variants
sections.content:
The method uses the same hash function for the message and HMAC. It uses the converted message hash so it can work with systems that give the signing engine an already-hashed message.

The RFC describes possible variants, such as adding non-repeating data, but those variants are no longer the defined deterministic DSA or ECDSA procedure and cannot be checked against this RFC's test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: The specified recipe supports existing signing systems and test vectors. Changing its inputs may be useful in some cases, but produces a different procedure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Deterministic signing removes the need for randomness during signature generation, not during key generation. The private key still needs a strong random source when it is created, and this RFC does not address key storage, access, or disposal.

The RFC warns that timing or power measurements may reveal information about the private key. Implementations should use defenses against side-channel leakage. It also notes that deterministic signatures may not suit some protocols that depend on randomized signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: Key creation still needs strong randomness. Implementations must also protect the signing operation from measurements that could reveal the private key.
